findings: Root cause of the reported bug: excludeDeleted() in genericSearch.ts hardcodes `where('deleted_at', 'IS', null)` and is applied uniformly (per the code's own comment) to both the orders and users searches. The users table has no deleted_at column at all (per the schema comment), and the ORM's unknownColumnMode: 'silent-skip', which is configured for all search endpoints, silently drops that predicate when it hits a nonexistent column instead of erroring. The result is that the users search runs with no deletion filter whatsoever, so soft-deleted users (is_deleted = true) leak into results — while orders, which really has deleted_at, is filtered correctly. This exactly matches the reported symptom.

Architectural inconsistency at the schema level: orders and users implement soft delete with two incompatible conventions (orders: nullable deleted_at TIMESTAMP tombstone; users: NOT NULL is_deleted BOOLEAN flag) with no shared abstraction or naming convention. genericSearch.ts's excludeDeleted() was written against only the timestamp-tombstone convention and then reused as a shared, table-agnostic helper across a schema that doesn't actually share that convention.

Fixing only the column-name mismatch is insufficient: excludeDeleted's predicate logic (`deleted_at IS NULL` for 'not deleted') is semantically specific to the nullable-timestamp pattern. Even if a deleted_at (or aliased) column were added to users, `IS NULL` does not correspond to the users table's boolean semantics (`is_deleted = false` means not deleted). A correct fix needs per-convention predicate logic (or a full schema-level normalization to one soft-delete convention), not just pointing the same WHERE clause at a different column name.

unknownColumnMode: 'silent-skip' is a systemic design risk beyond this one bug: it was adopted specifically to prevent 500s for optional, user-supplied filter columns that may not exist on a given table, but it is applied through the exact same query-building path as excludeDeleted, a mandatory, correctness/security-critical predicate. Nothing in genericSearch.ts distinguishes 'safe to silently drop' (an optional user filter) from 'must never silently drop' (a system-enforced visibility/deletion filter). Any other invariant filter added to this shared search path in the future (e.g., tenant scoping, access-control predicates) is equally exposed to being silently neutered — with no error and no log signal — whenever it's run against a table missing the expected column.

Missing safeguard: there is no schema-aware check or test asserting that excludeDeleted actually narrows results per table (e.g., validating the exclusion column exists before executing, or a test that soft-deleted users are excluded from search). That gap is precisely why a filter that has been a silent no-op for every users-table search went undetected until support reported it manually.
